summary: Many peer-to-peer streaming systems use proprietary protocols. This informational document identifies the problems that causes and proposes the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol (PPSP), including a tracker protocol and a peer protocol. It discusses scope, requirements, and use cases.

plainLanguage.summary: Streaming where viewers share pieces with each other works better with common rules. This explains why and what the rules should do.

questions: why do p2p streaming systems need standards
what is a swarm in p2p streaming
subtitle: A standard protocol to replace proprietary peer-to-peer streaming systems.

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer streaming systems on the Internet mostly use proprietary protocols, causing inefficiency, integration difficulties with CDNs, and higher deployment costs.
tldr.mechanism: PPSP standardizes signaling between tracking servers and peers, and between peers themselves, to enable interoperable P2P streaming for both live and video-on-demand content.
tldr.outcome: A common protocol simplifies development, reduces vendor lock-in, improves CDN cooperation, and allows ISPs to deploy single caches and proxies that work with all PPSP-compatible systems.

today: RFC 6972 identifies the requirements that standardized P2P streaming protocols should meet. The work has influenced subsequent standards efforts to define concrete PPSP mechanisms, moving the ecosystem away from purely proprietary solutions toward open protocols.

sections.title: The Problem With Proprietary Protocols
sections.content:
Peer-to-peer streaming has become a major part of Internet traffic, with systems distributing live streams and video files across networks by having viewers share content with each other. However, almost all P2P streaming systems today use their own proprietary protocols, meaning each application or service uses different rules and signals.

This fragmentation creates three major problems. First, ISPs that want to reduce traffic by caching frequently viewed content must deploy different cache systems for each P2P application. Second, Content Distribution Networks (CDNs) struggle to work efficiently with P2P systems because every protocol is different. Third, the lock-in effects of proprietary protocols make it expensive and difficult for multiple providers to collaborate on streaming delivery across regions or networks.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone building a video-sharing app invents their own rules, stores have to learn each set of rules. It is much simpler if everyone follows the same rules.

sections.title: How PPSP Works
sections.content:
PPSP addresses these problems by defining two complementary protocols. The tracker protocol handles communication between peers and a tracking service that knows which peers have content. The peer protocol handles direct communication between peers to share chunk availability and content pieces.

The tracker protocol works as a request-response mechanism. When a peer joins a swarm (a group sharing the same content), it queries the tracker for a list of other peers who have the chunks it needs. The tracker can optimize this list based on factors like peer quality and network location. The peer protocol, modeled as a gossip-style protocol, allows peers to periodically exchange information about which chunks they have available, enabling decentralized content discovery and transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The tracker is like a librarian who tells you which neighbors have the book you want. The peer protocol is how neighbors tell each other what books they have so they can trade with each other.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
PPSP defines several key terms. A chunk is the basic unit of content, ranging from kilobytes to megabytes depending on the system. A swarm is a group of peers exchanging chunks of the same content. A peer both receives and shares content; a client only receives. A super-node is a high-capacity peer deployed by ISPs to provide stable distribution points.

Content must be uniquely identified by a swarm ID, and each chunk within a swarm has a unique chunk ID. Every peer needs a unique peer ID so others can identify it. This standardized identification enables any conforming PPSP implementation to discover and communicate with any other.
sections.plainLanguage: A chunk is a piece of the video. A swarm is all the people currently watching and sharing that video. Each person and each piece gets a number so everyone knows what they are talking about.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
PPSP enables several new deployment models. Worldwide streaming cooperation allows providers in different regions to use the same PPSP tracker and peer protocols to reach audiences globally, optimizing peer selection across borders. CDN and P2P integration lets CDN nodes act as super-nodes within swarms, improving quality of service while keeping bandwidth efficient through P2P sharing. Cross-device streaming allows the same content to be shared between PCs, mobile phones, and set-top boxes with heterogeneous capabilities and network conditions.

ISPs can also deploy P2P caches that intercept requests and fetch content on behalf of peers, reducing inter-network traffic while acting as super-nodes themselves. Proxy services in home networks or browsers can use PPSP to enable older devices or web applications to participate in P2P streaming without modification.
sections.plainLanguage: PPSP lets streaming systems share pieces anywhere in the world, work alongside companies that cache videos, and handle smartphones and computers at the same time. ISPs can intercept that traffic and serve it locally without breaking the system.

sections.title: Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
PPSP has strict operational and security requirements. Trackers must handle queries and report peer activity; the protocol must be lightweight so a single tracker can serve millions of peers. Tracker responses must be tailored, considering peer preferences and network performance. Peers must report chunk availability changes frequently and efficiently, using compact representations of which chunks they hold.

Security is critical. The system must support closed swarms where only authenticated peers can join, with optional encryption of data between peers. Chunk integrity must be verifiable so corrupted or malicious chunks can be detected and rejected. Mechanisms must prevent peers from spoofing information about other peers or spreading false chunk availability, and the system must scale well as the number of peers grows, even when security mechanisms are applied.
sections.plainLanguage: The tracker cannot be slow or it will break under the load of millions of people asking for lists. Peers need to quickly tell each other which pieces they have. The system must prevent cheaters from lying about what they have or pretending to be someone else.
